passage: In the corridor outside the Class 5 room of their Kochi school, Jomon spotted it: a hundred-rupee note, folded in four, half under the notice board. His heart raced. That could be a whole comic book. Or ten packets of spicy chips. Or the yo-yo with lights. He picked it up, and his fingers curled around it. Devika came round the corner. 'What's that?' 'Nothing.' Then, 'I found money.' She looked at it. 'Someone must be looking for it. Remember when Ammu lost her fees money?' Jomon remembered her crying. He looked at the note one more time, imagining the yo-yo. Then he walked to the staffroom and gave it to Lissy Miss. 'Found near the notice board.' She wrote his name in the lost-property book.

qa.q: Where did Jomon find the note?
qa.a: Half under the notice board in the corridor.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when his fingers curled around the note?
qa.a: Excited and tempted, his heart racing with ideas of what he could buy.

qa.q: What helped Jomon make the wise choice?
qa.a: Devika's question and remembering Ammu crying over lost fees money, which led him to hand it to Lissy Miss.

qa.q: How might the owner of the note feel?
qa.a: Worried and upset, the way Ammu was, until it is returned.

grounding: A boy who finds a note at school feels the pull to spend it, then hands it to a teacher.

passage:
'Tanuja, look!' Salma held up a crumpled hundred-rupee note by the drinking-water tap.
'Whoa! Finders keepers?'
'I don't know.' Salma's heart was thumping. 'I could buy the gel pens. The whole set.'
'Do it. Nobody saw.'
'But what if it's someone's bus money? Or lunch?'
'Then they should have been careful.'
Salma turned the note over in her fingers. 'If I lost a hundred, I'd be crying in the toilet.'
Tanuja went quiet. 'Yeah. Me too.'
'Let's ask around first. Then the office.'
They asked three girls at the tap. The third one, a small Class 3 girl, burst into tears of relief. 'It's my Amma's, for the milk!'
Salma handed it over. The gel pens could wait.

qa.q: Where did Salma find the note?
qa.a: By the drinking-water tap.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when she first held the note?
qa.a: Excited and tempted, her heart thumping at the idea of buying the gel pens.

qa.q: What did Salma choose to do, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Ask whose it was before going to the office, because it might be someone's bus or lunch money.

qa.q: How did the Class 3 girl feel when she got the note back?
qa.a: Hugely relieved; she burst into tears because it was her Amma's milk money.

grounding: A girl tempted by a found note asks around and returns it to its young owner.

passage: On the metro platform in Delhi, Noor found a small plastic pouch with fifty rupees and a school ID card inside: 'Aman Verma, Class 2'. The photo showed a boy with a gap-toothed grin. Noor imagined him standing at his school gate right now, patting his pockets, his face crumpling. He might be scared to tell his mother. Maybe it was his canteen money for the whole week. Her own stomach twisted just thinking of it. 'Should we just keep it?' her friend Shreya asked. 'He's probably so worried,' Noor said. They showed it to the metro guard, who called the school printed on the card. That evening Noor's mother got a call from Aman's father, thanking them. Noor felt warm all the way to her toes.

qa.q: Whose name was on the ID card?
qa.a: Aman Verma, Class 2.

qa.q: Why did Noor's stomach twist?
qa.a: She imagined Aman's fear at losing the money and felt sorry for him.

qa.q: How did Noor return the pouch?
qa.a: She showed it to the metro guard, who called the school printed on the card.

qa.q: How might Aman feel when the pouch comes back?
qa.a: Relieved and happy after being worried about the lost money.

grounding: A girl who finds a small boy's lost money imagines his worry, and returning it feels warm rather than like a loss.

passage:
'Urmila, someone dropped this under the bus seat.' Kiran held up a little red coin purse with a zip.
Urmila peeked inside. 'Coins, a folded note, and a paper. "Rehan, 1B. Money for Nani's medicine."'
Kiran's face fell. 'Oh no. He's so small. Remember when you lost your bus pass and cried all the way home?'
'Don't remind me.' Urmila shuddered. 'He'll get scolded. Or worse, his Nani won't get her medicine.'
'He's probably searching his bag right now, thinking he's in so much trouble.'
'Then let's find him. 1B gets off at the next stop.'
The bus braked. Kiran ran down the aisle. 'Rehan? Is anyone Rehan?' A tiny boy looked up, eyes red. Kiran held out the purse. His whole face opened like a window.

qa.q: What was written on the paper in the purse?
qa.a: Rehan, 1B. Money for Nani's medicine.

qa.q: Why did Kiran's face fall when Urmila read the paper?
qa.a: Kiran felt worried and sorry for small Rehan, imagining how scared he must be.

qa.q: What made returning the purse feel simple?
qa.a: Imagining Rehan's fear and his Nani's medicine turned it into a kindness, not a loss.

qa.q: How did Rehan feel before and after the purse came back?
qa.a: Scared and tearful before, then relieved and delighted when his face opened like a window 😊

grounding: Two children who find a small boy's purse imagine his worry and hurry to return it.

passage: Last summer, my friends and I found a fifty-rupee note in the dust behind the cricket ground. I'm Dhruv. Straight away Aman shouted, 'Finders keepers! Chips and cold drinks for everyone!' and the others cheered. I wanted to cheer too. Everyone was looking at me, because I was the one holding it. My mouth went dry. I kept thinking of the old watchman, who had been searching the grass all morning. 'I think it might be the watchman's,' I said. 'I'm going to ask him.' Aman groaned and called me a goody-goody. But on the way, Ujjwal fell into step beside me. 'I was thinking the same thing,' he whispered. 'I just didn't want to say it.' The watchman nearly cried when we gave it back.

qa.q: Where did they find the note?
qa.a: In the dust behind the cricket ground.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when everyone looked at the note?
qa.a: Torn and nervous, mouth dry, wanting to fit in but thinking of the watchman.

qa.q: How did Dhruv decline without a fight?
qa.a: By calmly saying it might be the watchman's and going to ask him.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel about Dhruv speaking up?
qa.a: Relieved; he had been thinking the same thing but hadn't dared to say it.

grounding: A child pressured by friends to keep found money politely declines, and one friend is quietly relieved.

passage:
Playground note, by Dilnaz Irani, lunch supervisor.
Near the swings today, a group of Class 5 children found a twenty-rupee note. I heard one shout, 'Finders keepers! Ice lollies!' and three others agreed at once. Vidya, who had picked it up, went very still. She looked from the group to the note and bit her lip. 'We should ask whose it is,' she said quietly. Two of them rolled their eyes. 'Don't be boring.' Vidya didn't argue. She just said, 'I'm giving it to the supervisor,' and walked to me. As she came, I noticed one of the group, Minal, trailing behind and letting out a long breath. The note belonged to a Class 2 child, who got it back before the bell.

qa.q: What did one child shout?
qa.a: 'Finders keepers! Ice lollies!'

qa.q: What did Vidya's stillness and bitten lip show?
qa.a: She felt torn between fitting in with the group and doing what was right.

qa.q: How did Vidya decline without a fight?
qa.a: She said once that they should ask whose it was, didn't argue, and simply walked the note to the supervisor.

qa.q: How might Minal have felt as she trailed behind?
qa.a: Relieved that someone had said it, since Minal let out a long breath.

grounding: A supervisor's note records a girl declining her friends' 'finders keepers' plan and handing in found money.

passage: At Samir Bhai's general store in their Lucknow colony, Naveen paid for a packet of bread with a fifty-rupee note. Samir Bhai, talking on his phone and weighing onions at the same time, pushed the change across the counter. Naveen counted it on the steps outside. Forty-five rupees. The bread cost twenty-five. He had twenty extra. Nobody would know. Samir Bhai was busy. But Naveen would know every time he walked past the shop. His cheeks went warm. He turned round and stood at the counter, feeling awkward. 'Bhaiya, you gave me twenty extra.' Samir Bhai stopped, counted, and laughed. 'Arre, thank you, beta! My head is full of onions today.' He handed Naveen a toffee. Naveen walked home feeling light as the bread.

qa.q: What did the bread cost?
qa.a: Twenty-five rupees.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel as he stood at the counter?
qa.a: Awkward, with warm cheeks, but sure he would know every time he passed the shop.

qa.q: What did Naveen do, and why?
qa.a: He returned the extra twenty because even if nobody else knew, he would.

qa.q: How did Samir Bhai react?
qa.a: He laughed, thanked Naveen, admitted he was distracted, and gave him a toffee.

grounding: A boy given extra change returns it because he would know, and feels awkward then light.

passage:
'That'll be thirty-five,' said the stationery uncle, and Ishita handed him a hundred.
He gave her back a small pile. Outside, Sonali counted it with her. 'Wait. This is seventy-five.'
'He gave me ten extra,' Ishita whispered.
'Lucky! That's a gel pen. Nobody will know.'
'I'll know.' Ishita's ears were hot. 'He'll count his box tonight and it'll be short.'
'He won't even remember us.'
'Still.' She pushed the door open again. The bell jingled, and she felt silly and a bit shaky. 'Uncle, you gave me too much. It should be sixty-five.'
He counted, blinked, then smiled. 'You're right. Thank you, bitiya. Not many children come back.'
Out on the pavement, Ishita laughed, suddenly light. Sonali nudged her. 'Okay, that felt good.'

qa.q: How much should the change have been?
qa.a: Sixty-five.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling as she pushed the door open again?
qa.a: Awkward, silly and a bit shaky, but sure it was right to return the money.

qa.q: Why did Ishita return the ten rupees even though nobody would know?
qa.a: Because she would know, and the shopkeeper's box would be short that night.

qa.q: How did the shopkeeper see Ishita coming back?
qa.a: With surprise and gratitude; he said not many children come back.

grounding: A girl given extra change by a shopkeeper returns it despite her friend's urging, and feels light afterwards.

passage: Akash had found a brown wallet on the seat of the auto that morning, full of cards and some cash, and had handed it to the society guard straight away. By evening, the owner had come by the flat to say thank you, and Papa knew everything. When Akash came home from cricket, Papa hugged him so hard his cap fell off. 'That's my boy!' Akash grinned, warm all over. At dinner, his little brother Mohit asked, 'Would you still have given it back if nobody said thank you?' Akash thought about it, chewing his roti. 'Yes. It wasn't mine.' He meant it. The hug had felt great. But he'd have felt worse keeping the wallet than he felt good being praised.

qa.q: Who did Akash hand the wallet to?
qa.a: The society guard.

qa.q: How did Akash feel when Papa hugged him?
qa.a: Proud and warm all over, happy to be praised.

qa.q: What does Akash's answer to Mohit show?
qa.a: That he returns things because it's right, not for praise; he would have done it anyway.

qa.q: How did Papa feel about Akash?
qa.a: Very proud; he hugged him so hard his cap fell off.

grounding: A boy whose father hugs him for returning a wallet enjoys the praise but knows he would have done it anyway.

passage:
'Ammi, guess what? I found a wallet at the bus stop and gave it to the conductor!'
Ammi dropped the ladle and hugged Salma tight. 'My honest girl! I'm telling your Khala.'
Her cousin Darshan, on the sofa, raised an eyebrow. 'You only did it so Ammi would hug you.'
Salma frowned. 'No, I didn't.'
'Would you have done it if nobody would ever find out?'
Salma thought about the wallet: the old photo of a baby inside, the bus pass. 'Yes. Someone's baby picture was in there.'
'Okay,' Darshan said. 'Then it counts.'
'Everything counts,' Ammi said, laughing. But later, Salma sat on the balcony and asked herself again. The hug had felt lovely. But the best part had been handing it over, before anyone knew.

qa.q: Who did Salma give the wallet to?
qa.a: The conductor.

qa.q: How did Salma feel when Ammi hugged her?
qa.a: Proud and loved; the hug felt lovely.

qa.q: What did Salma realise on the balcony?
qa.a: That the best part was handing the wallet over before anyone knew, so the honesty mattered more than the praise.

qa.q: How does Darshan test Salma's reason?
qa.a: He wonders whether she did it only for praise and asks if she would do it with nobody finding out.

grounding: A girl praised for returning a wallet reflects that honesty matters to her even without praise.

passage:
Monday. Yamini found a ten-rupee coin under the classroom bench and asked around. It belonged to little Shreya from Class 2, who hugged her and said, 'Thank you, Didi!' with a huge smile. Yamini glowed all day.
Thursday. Yamini found a lost pencil box in the library. She carried it to its owner, a Class 4 boy, and waited for the hug. He just grabbed it, muttered 'thanks' and ran off. Yamini felt oddly cheated.
Friday. At home she told Amma, 'Why didn't he smile like Shreya?' Amma raised an eyebrow. 'Did you return it for a smile?' Yamini thought. 'No. For him.' 'Then you already got what you wanted.' Yamini laughed. It was true. The box was back with its owner.

qa.q: What did Shreya say to Yamini?
qa.a: 'Thank you, Didi!'

qa.q: How did Yamini feel on Thursday when the boy ran off?
qa.a: Oddly cheated and disappointed, because she had been expecting a hug or a big smile.

qa.q: What did Amma's question help Yamini see?
qa.a: That she returns things for the owner, not for thanks, so doing right is its own reward.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel when her coin came back?
qa.a: Happy and grateful; she hugged Yamini with a huge smile.

grounding: Over a week a girl enjoys a child's thanks for returned money, then learns not to expect a reward every time.

passage: 'Mohit, you're sulking because the boy didn't even say thank you properly? Let your Akash Chacha tell you something. When I was nine, I found an old lady's cloth purse in the vegetable market and ran after her with it. She held my face in both hands and gave me a whole packet of peanut chikki. I felt like a king. After that, whenever I found anything, a pen, a hanky, I rushed to return it and waited for my chikki. It never came. Once a man just grabbed his umbrella and walked off. I was so annoyed! Then my grandfather said, "Are you honest, or are you selling honesty for chikki?" That stung. But he was right. The good feeling is the reward, beta. The chikki was just extra.'

qa.q: What did the old lady give young Akash?
qa.a: A whole packet of peanut chikki.

qa.q: How did young Akash feel when the man walked off with his umbrella?
qa.a: Annoyed and let down, because he had started expecting a reward.

qa.q: What question in the story changed Akash's thinking?
qa.a: His grandfather asking whether he was honest or selling honesty for chikki.

qa.q: How did the old lady feel when Akash ran after her?
qa.a: Grateful and touched; she held his face in both hands.

grounding: An uncle recalls being rewarded for returning a purse, starting to expect rewards, and learning doing right is its own reward.

passage:
'Did you hear it?' Trisha whispered as they came out of the temple, still buzzing. 'When everyone sang the aarti together, the whole floor felt like it was humming.'
Siddharth nodded, licking prasad off his fingers. 'I got goosebumps.'
'Me too. Like we were one big voice.' Trisha turned to Dida. 'Dida, why do we wave the lamp in circles?'
'Hm?' Dida smiled. 'Nobody asks me that any more.'
'Is it okay to ask?'
'Of course. Asking means you care.' Dida sat down on the temple step. 'My mother said the circles show that God is all around, with no beginning and no end. Some people say other things. You can think about it yourself.'
Trisha watched the last lamp flicker inside. 'I like the no-end idea,' she said, and hummed the aarti tune all the way home.

qa.q: What did Siddharth lick off his fingers?
qa.a: Prasad.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel when everyone sang the aarti together?
qa.a: Excited and connected, as if they were one big voice; she got goosebumps.

qa.q: What does Trisha add to belonging, besides singing?
qa.a: She asks why things are done, like waving the lamp in circles, and thinks about the answer herself.

qa.q: How did Dida feel about Trisha's question?
qa.a: Pleased; she smiled because nobody asked her any more, and said asking means you care 🙂

grounding: A girl feels part of something bigger when everyone sings at the temple, and also asks why things are done.

passage: Every Christmas Eve, our whole church in Kottayam sings 'Silent Night' with the lights off and only candles burning. I'm Thomas, and the first year I was old enough to hold my own candle, I nearly cried. Hundreds of voices, old and young, all in the dark together, and mine one of them. It felt like being inside something huge and kind. My friend Damini, who is Hindu, came with us that year and hummed the tune without the words. Afterwards I asked Father Joseph why we turn the lights off. I was worried it was a silly question. He said, 'Good question. The candles remind us of one small light coming into the dark.' I think about that every year now, instead of only singing.

qa.q: What song does the church sing with the lights off?
qa.a: 'Silent Night'.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel singing with the candles?
qa.a: Moved and part of something huge and kind; Thomas nearly cried.

qa.q: What did Thomas do besides singing along?
qa.a: Asked Father Joseph why the lights are turned off, and now thinks about the meaning every year.

qa.q: How did Father Joseph see Thomas's question?
qa.a: As a good question worth answering, not a silly one.

grounding: A child feels deep belonging singing with the church community, and also asks why things are done.

passage: At dusk in their village near Kolhapur, Aaji lit the small brass lamp by the tulsi pot and sat Aditi down beside her on the courtyard floor. 'Today I'll teach you the prayer my own Aaji taught me.' She sang it slowly, line by line, her thin voice wobbling on the high notes, and her eyes shone in the lamplight. Aditi repeated each line, getting some of the words mixed up. Aaji laughed and squeezed her hand. Aditi felt warm, as if she were holding one end of a long rope that went back and back. Her cousin Rekha was sniggering from the doorway, but Aditi didn't care. Later, as they rolled cotton wicks, Aditi asked, 'Aaji, what does the third line mean?' Aaji beamed. 'Ask me anything. That's how you keep it.'

qa.q: Where did Aaji light the lamp?
qa.a: By the tulsi pot.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel learning the prayer?
qa.a: Loved and rooted, as if holding one end of a long rope that went back through the family.

qa.q: How did Aditi take in the prayer with respect and curiosity?
qa.a: She repeated each line carefully and later asked Aaji what the third line meant.

qa.q: How did Aaji feel when Aditi asked a question?
qa.a: Delighted; she beamed and said asking is how you keep it.

grounding: A village girl learns a prayer from her grandmother, feels loved and rooted, and asks questions about it.

passage: In Buenos Aires, whenever Valentina stayed over at her abuela's flat, they sat together on the edge of the high bed before sleep. Abuela took out her old wooden rosary, smooth from years of fingers, and taught Valentina the short prayer she had said every night since she was a girl. Her eyes shone in the lamplight as she said the words, soft and sure. Valentina said them after her, slowly. She didn't understand every word. But she understood Abuela's hand, warm around hers, and the feeling that she was part of something that had started long before her. Her cousin Javier peeked in, yawning. Valentina whispered, 'Abuela, tomorrow can you tell me what "grace" means?' Abuela kissed her forehead. 'Tomorrow, and every day you ask.'

qa.q: What was Abuela's rosary made of?
qa.a: Old wood, smooth from years of fingers.

qa.q: What was Valentina feeling as she said the prayer?
qa.a: Loved and connected, part of something that had started long before her.

qa.q: How did Valentina respect the prayer while staying curious?
qa.a: She said it carefully after Abuela and asked to learn what 'grace' means the next day.

qa.q: How did Abuela respond to Valentina's question?
qa.a: Warmly; she kissed her forehead and welcomed questions every day.

grounding: A girl in Argentina learns her grandmother's bedtime prayer, feels loved and rooted, and plans to ask what it means.

passage: Every Sunday in Cape Town, Camila sat cross-legged in the church hall while Brother Thabo told stories: a shepherd searching all night for one lost sheep, a stranger stopping to help a hurt man on the road. Camila believed every word. She loved how his voice went soft at the sad parts. One Sunday a visiting speaker came instead and said children who asked questions would be punished. Camila's stomach went tight. That night she told her mum. 'Brother Thabo never says scary things. He says God is like the shepherd.' Mum hugged her. 'Good noticing. Good teachers make you kinder, not frightened. And you can always ask me.' The next Sunday Brother Thabo was back, and Camila asked him why the shepherd didn't give up. He smiled.

qa.q: What did the shepherd search for all night?
qa.a: One lost sheep.

qa.q: What was Camila feeling when the visiting speaker talked about punishment?
qa.a: Frightened and uneasy; her stomach went tight.

qa.q: What did Camila learn to notice about teachers of faith?
qa.a: That good teachers make you kinder, not frightened, and that she can ask her mum about anything worrying.

qa.q: How did Mum see Camila telling her?
qa.a: As good noticing; she hugged her and invited her always to ask.

grounding: A girl who trusts her Sunday school teacher's stories begins to notice that good teaching promotes kindness, not fear.

passage: Every Saturday morning, Binita went to the children's class at the community temple hall, where Lokesh-ji told stories from the Ramayana with his hands flying. Binita believed every word: the flying monkey, the stones floating on the sea. Afterwards he always asked, 'So what did we learn about being kind?' and everyone had to give one small idea, like sharing tiffin or helping at home. Once Binita put her hand up and asked, 'But why did the stones float?' Some kids laughed. Lokesh-ji didn't. 'Good question. What do you think?' He never asked the children to keep secrets from their parents, and he never made anyone scared. Binita trusted him the way she trusted the morning sun. Walking home, she told Papa her one small idea: helping Nani with the washing.

qa.q: Which stories did Lokesh-ji tell?
qa.a: Stories from the Ramayana.

qa.q: How did Binita feel about Lokesh-ji?
qa.a: Trusting and safe, the way she trusted the morning sun.

qa.q: What signs showed Lokesh-ji's teaching was healthy?
qa.a: He asked about kindness, welcomed questions, and never asked for secrets or made anyone scared.

qa.q: How did Lokesh-ji respond when kids laughed at Binita's question?
qa.a: He didn't laugh; he called it a good question and asked what she thought.

grounding: A girl trusts her temple class teacher, whose teaching invites kindness and questions and never fear or secrecy.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, by Deepak Rao, Monday dinner.
Every evening, before the dal and rice are served, Jeevan (Class 4) closes his eyes and whispers a short prayer of thanks. Tonight I heard him: 'Thank you for Amma and Appa and this food.' He looked peaceful, then dug in happily. Tonight, too, the new boy at the end of the table had spilled his plate and was sitting with nothing, eyes down. Jeevan noticed. He pushed half his rice onto a clean plate and slid it across. 'I already said thank you for it,' he said with a shrug. 'Now it's for sharing.' I asked the kitchen to bring a fresh plate for the new boy, and I will quietly mention Jeevan's kindness to his parents.

qa.q: What does Jeevan whisper before dinner?
qa.a: 'Thank you for Amma and Appa and this food.'

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as he prayed?
qa.a: Peaceful and grateful, thankful for his parents and his food.

qa.q: How did Jeevan turn gratitude into action?
qa.a: He shared half his rice with the new boy who had spilled his plate.

qa.q: How might the new boy feel when the plate slid across?
qa.a: Surprised and relieved, and less alone after sitting with nothing.

grounding: A hostel warden's note shows a boy who thanks God before eating and turns that gratitude into sharing.

passage:
Sunday night
Dear diary, Yash here. Tonight before dinner we all held hands and Dadi said thank you to God, like always, for the food and for all of us being together. Usually I just mumble along because I'm hungry. Tonight I actually thought about it. Chole, hot rotis, Mummy, Papa, Dadi, even my annoying sister. I felt warm and a bit lucky. Then I remembered Tanvir, the watchman's son, sitting by the gate earlier with only a packet of biscuits. After dinner I asked Mummy if I could take him some chole and two rotis. She packed them in a steel box. Tanvir grinned and said chole was his favourite. I think saying thank you and doing something should go together.

qa.q: What was Tanvir eating earlier by the gate?
qa.a: Only a packet of biscuits.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when really thinking about the prayer?
qa.a: Warm and a bit lucky, grateful for the food and the family 🙏

qa.q: How did Yash turn gratitude into action?
qa.a: By asking Mummy to pack chole and rotis for Tanvir and taking them to him.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel when the steel box arrived?
qa.a: Happy; he grinned and said chole was his favourite.

grounding: A child who gives thanks before a family meal turns the gratitude into sharing food with someone who has less.
